chunks: ESC components and subsystems. The question: What components/subsystems does an ESC have?
An ESC can be split into four groups of parts. The power path carries the battery current to the motor. The control path decides what to switch and when.
The sensing parts measure the motor and battery. The support parts make small supply voltages and keep everything safe.
Think of the ESC as a body. The MOSFETs (power switches) are the muscles that do the heavy work. The microcontroller (a small computer chip) is the brain that decides what to do.
The sensing circuits are the senses, telling the brain what is happening. The regulators are the digestion, turning the battery's energy into the small supplies the brain needs.
The analogy has one gap: the whole thing also needs fast capacitors close to the muscles.
The ESC as a set of blocks.
Power flows top to bottom through the bridge to the motor; information flows back from the back-EMF network and the shunt to the MCU, which closes the loop through the gate drivers.
The regulators hang off the DC link.
DC link capacitors: charge stores at the battery input that supply the sudden bursts of current. Gate driver: a chip that switches the MOSFETs quickly and safely.
Bootstrap: a small capacitor and diode that give the upper switches the extra voltage they need to turn on. Shunt: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
BEC: a regulator that makes 5 volts for outside electronics.
Follow one command through. The throttle signal goes into the microcontroller. The microcontroller sends six fast on/off (PWM) signals to the gate driver.
The gate driver switches the six MOSFETs, which push current to the motor.
A 1 milliohms shunt carrying 30 amps produces 30 millivolts (30 amps times 1 milliohms), which a comparator (a circuit that flags when a voltage crosses a limit) watches for overcurrent.
Resistor dividers on each motor wire let the firmware see back-EMF. A regulator makes 5 volts and 3. 3 volts for the logic.
That is the whole idea: power, control, sensing and support, all linked by firmware.
"An ESC has four groups of parts. The power path: input connector, DC-link capacitors and a three-phase bridge of six MOSFETs.
The control path: a microcontroller running commutation, with a gate driver, bootstrap and dead-time between it and the FETs.
The sensing: back-EMF dividers into comparators or ADC, a shunt for current, and voltage and temperature sensors.
And the support: a BEC and logic regulators, throttle input conditioning, telemetry and protection firmware."
Quick check. Why are capacitors placed right next to the ESC's MOSFETs?
